connector: Well now. It’s Matthew. Marilla told me the whole business about the tea, the night it happened, and I’m ashamed to say I laughed. Not at Anne. At the size of the trouble a bottle can make. She’s gone back to school since, on her own account, with her books on her arm and her mouth set. I dunno what she’s planning. Something.

guide2.label: Matthew · before you open the book

rwm.label: Matthew · about Read like a Writer

transcripts.welcome: Well now, it’s Matthew, and I’m your guide for these two chapters. The question up there says the hard part of Anne’s past turns into a gift. I dunno how yet. I can believe it, though. Anne never had much, and she made the most of every bit. So as you go, keep an eye on who freezes and who moves. Then there’s doing words to find, and some c’s and g’s that don’t behave.
transcripts.wgrd: Marilla and I look at Anne and see two different girls. Marilla sees the mistakes. I see, well, I dunno what I see. The girl. And it’s not that one of us is wrong. It’s what each of us has lived through. So do what the box says. One sentence for each person, then ask what they’ve been through that makes them see it that way. That’s the whole gap, most times.
transcripts.dol: Marilla does the grammar in this house. But I can hear a sentence that runs on too long, the way I can hear a wagon that needs grease. The bottom one is two thoughts with no stop between them. Read it out loud and stop where you’d take a breath. That’s your period. Then the next word stands up straight with a capital letter. Anne’s name wants one too.
transcripts.guide1: Well now. Four boxes, and I’m no scholar, so I’ll say what I’d do. Two are matching, tap one thing, then tap its partner. Two are tapping words in a row, and in those you’re hunting, so don’t tap the first thing that looks likely. Read the whole row first. The spelling one is looking for the words that break the rule, not the ones that keep it. Easy to get that backwards.
transcripts.morphology: Four ways to say not. I dunno why a word needs four, one would do me. But there’s a rule about which one goes where, and the rule is in the little words in brackets. Say those out loud, and look at the first letter of each one after the chunk comes off. That letter is what you’re matching, not the meaning. The meanings are all the same. That’s the trick of it.
transcripts.vocabulary: You met these four yesterday. Well now, I forget words the day after I learn them, so here’s what I do. Say the word, then say the meaning, and listen to whether they sit together. If it sounds like two strangers, it probably is. Do the pair you’re surest of first, and then the next, and the last two nearly match themselves. And if you get one wrong, read the little line that comes up.
transcripts.grammar: There’s more than one doing word in that sentence, and I’d have read it and just nodded. So go slow. Ask of each word, is somebody doing this right now? A name isn’t. A little word like and isn’t. Then check the end of each one you tapped against who’s doing it, one person or more than one. I dunno the rule for that. Anne does. You will, by the end of the week.
transcripts.spelling: Most of those words do what the rule says. One or two don’t, and those are the ones you tap. So say each word, listen for the hard sound or the soft one, then look at the letter after the c or the g and ask if the rule would have guessed right. When it wouldn’t, that’s your word. Leave the good ones be. Tapping a good one costs you.
transcripts.guide2: The box says courage is doing the hard thing while you’re still afraid. Well now, I’m not a brave man. Going up those stairs to talk Anne into apologizing, when Marilla had told me not to interfere, that was about my limit. But I went. So watch for that. Not somebody who isn’t scared. Somebody who is, and does the thing anyway. And watch what the other people do while she’s doing it.
transcripts.read: One stop, at the end of the first chapter, and it asks whether a person can enjoy being sad. Well now, Anne can enjoy pretty near anything. When you get there, ask yourself if she’s only sad, or something else along with it. Then read the second chapter straight through, no stopping, and keep count of who moves and who stands still. That’s what the reading move is about.
transcripts.rwm: Well now, that’s Anne all over. Sorry and thrilled in the one breath. The sentence works because the although part holds the feeling you’d expect, and the main part holds the one you wouldn’t. Cover the first half with your finger and it’s just a girl enjoying herself. Put it back and she’s a person. When you write yours, put the ordinary feeling first, and save the surprising one for the end.
transcripts.guide3: I went to Carmody for the doctor and there wasn’t one, so I went clear to Spencervale, and it was the small hours when we got back. And it was over. Anne had done it. I walked her home and she talked the whole way, and I let her. Now it’s your turn to say what you noticed, and I dunno that you need to say much. Just say it with the book open.
transcripts.chapter: The first question is about that farewell, and I wasn’t at the spring, but I heard about it at supper. Look at the words Anne chose and ask why a person picks those. The second is where her skill came from. She tells Diana, not the doctor. Find that. The third is about Mrs. Barry. I was doing chores when she came. Marilla heard it. Quote the moment, not the feeling.
transcripts.wordconn: Your grammar answer is saved. When I tell about that night it all comes out in the past, went and drove. The page wanted you to find the doing words that happen now, and I dunno why, but it makes a story feel closer. Take the verb you tapped, ask who’s doing it, and ask whether the ending fits that person. Then look at your own writing and try one sentence in the now.
transcripts.workshop: Sam’s boy wants to make the team, and part of him wants to skip it. Well now, I wanted to keep Anne, and couldn’t say so out loud. That’s a want and a wall in the one person. Write your first scene so we know where your kid is and what they want. Then one line that hints at the thing in the way. One line. Don’t explain it. Let it show.

a.raw: anne knows what to do for croup she races through the snow
a.fixed: Anne knows what to do for croup. She races through the snow.
a.why: A capital letter on the name Anne, a period to close the first thought, a capital S to start the next sentence, and a period at the end.

b.raw: matthew harnesses the sorrel mare he drives off for the doctor
b.fixed: Matthew harnesses the sorrel mare. He drives off for the doctor.
b.why: The same pattern: a capital on the name Matthew, a period where the first thought ends, a capital H to start the next sentence, and a period at the end.

scholar.journal-q1: … and say what the big words do for Anne that plain ones could not.
scholar.journal-q2: … then say what Anne had that Young Mary Joe did not, in one word, and prove it.
scholar.journal-q3: … and say which changed more, Mrs. Barry or Anne, and how you can tell.

match.cordial: Cordial has cor inside it, the Latin word for heart. Look for the meaning about being warm-hearted.
match.relent: Relent is what a hard person does when they finally soften. Look for the meaning about changing your mind.
match.incapable: Incapable starts with the “not” chunk and has capable inside it. Look for the meaning about not being able.
match.inexorable: Inexorable also starts with the “not” chunk, and the rest means “able to be begged.” Look for the meaning about refusing to give in.

notes.wgrd: When views split, ask why. What a person has lived through shapes what they see.
vocab: warmly friendly (also a sweet drink offered to friends)
to soften, become less harsh, or change your mind
refusing to give in or change; unable to be moved by pleading
notes.wordParts: il-, ir-, im-, and in- all mean “not”: il- before l (illegal), ir- before r (irregular), im- before b, m, or p (impossible), in- before other letters (incorrect).
notes.grammar: Present-tense verbs must agree with their subject: I, you, we, they walk; he, she, it walks. Use is or are + -ing for something happening right now (she is walking).
notes.spelling: c and g are usually soft (/s/ and /j/) before e, i, or y (cellar, gentle, energy) and hard before a, o, or u (cordial, golden). A few words break the rule (get, girl).
